title: Republicans get bad news on inflation
content: A Cygnal poll released in September 2025 shows that 39.6 percent of Americans now blame Republicans for rising inflation, overtaking Democrats at 36.5 percent, a shift from the previous year when Democrats were blamed by 46.3 percent and Republicans by 25.5 percent. The poll also reports that 54.3 percent of respondents say inflation is getting worse, compared with 23.4 percent who say it is improving, and 20.5 percent who think it is about the same. Inflation has risen to roughly 3.4 percent annually, with tariffs contributing about 2.3 percent in the short term and an average household loss of $3,800. Housing costs have increased, requiring an annual income of $114,000 to afford a median‑priced home, up 70 percent since 2019. The U.S. jobs market added only 22,000 jobs in August 2025, after a loss of 13,000 in June, and the unemployment rate rose to 4.3 percent, the highest since 2021. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) revised its April 2024‑March 2025 jobs figure down by 911,000, the largest revision on record. Trump’s White House has blamed the Biden administration for the BLS revision, with Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt stating, 'Today, the BLS released the largest downward revision on record proving that President Trump was right: Biden's economy was a disaster and the BLS is broken.' Trump has also criticized Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell, calling him 'Mr. Too Late' and demanding rate cuts. Despite economic anxiety, Republicans still hold a narrow trust edge on economic stewardship, with voters four points more likely to trust the GOP than Democrats on the economy and jobs. Trump’s approval rating has fallen to 44 percent approval and 52 percent disapproval, a net rating of –8 points, up from an all‑time low of –11 points in August. The Federal Open Market Committee will meet on September 19 to decide on the key interest rate, currently targeted at 4.25‑4.5 percent.

title: Americans expect inflation to be far higher than it really is, polling shows
content: The University of Michigan’s inflation‑expectation survey shows that Americans over‑estimate inflation by a wide margin since Donald Trump’s second term began. In December 2024, respondents expected 2.8 % inflation while the CPI was 2.7 %; by May 2025, expectations had risen to 6.6 % against an actual 2.4 %. The article cites the survey question, ‘By about what percent do you expect prices to go up/down on the average, during the next 12 months?’, the decline in the dollar (from 1.00 to 0.85 euro, a 15 % fall), the Trump administration’s high tariffs, and the ‘big beautiful bill’ that would add $3 trillion to debt 2025‑2034 and $12.1 trillion 2025‑2055, according to Yale University Budget Lab. It also notes that the public’s inflation expectations track closely with President Trump’s job approval, suggesting that higher expectations could hurt his reelection prospects. The piece uses data from the Consumer Price Index, the Federal Reserve, and YouGov polls to support its claims, and mentions the stalled appointment of Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook as a source of economic uncertainty.

title: Inflation Is Down Since January and Should Keep Improving
content: Despite predictions of runaway inflation, the latest data show that inflation has decreased since January and is expected to continue improving. The energy agenda of President Trump has played a key role in bringing inflation under control, as reducing energy prices puts downward pressure on prices everywhere. Energy prices rose in June due to geopolitical fears and disruptions, but have since come back down, including for consumer staples like gasoline. Wholesale prices have also remained flat since January, with a cumulative wholesale inflation rate of just 0.1 percent during Mr. Trump's first five months in office. This stands in contrast to the 8.5 percent annualized wholesale inflation rate when Mr. Trump took office. The 'experts' who predicted high inflation have been proven wrong, and there is reason to believe that consumer price inflation will slow further later this year. Mr. Trump's energy agenda is a key ingredient in the mix, and with continued reform, spending cuts, tax relief, and fixing the Fed, America can truly enter a Golden Age.

title: Trump has repeatedly said the U.S. has "no inflation." He's wrong
content: The article refutes President Donald Trump’s repeated claim that the United States has ‘no inflation.’  Trump said, ‘Even people that were against the tariffs, now they see the way they’re working. And by the way, with no inflation, with no problem, we’re just building up cash…’ (Sept. 19).  White House spokesperson Kush Desai echoed this, stating, ‘President Trump is right: The days of Joe Biden’s debilitating inflation crisis are over. Since President Trump took office, inflation has been tracking at a low and stable 2.3 percent annualized rate…’ (July 1‑present).  However, data show the inflation rate is far from zero: the consumer price index (CPI) rose 2.9 % year‑over‑year in August, and the CPI‑minus‑food‑and‑energy index was 3.5 % in July.  The Federal Reserve’s price‑stability target is about 2 %, and the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) index was 2.6 % in July, above the target.  Inflation has accelerated over the past four months, with categories such as electricity (+6.2 % from Aug 24 to Aug 25), used vehicles (+6 %), medical care (+3.4 %), groceries (+2.7 %) and durable goods (+1.9 %) all rising.  Economist Gary Burtless noted, ‘Consumer price inflation is not zero, under any plausibly complete definition covering all the goods and services Americans purchase.’  George Washington University economist Tara Sinclair added, ‘I think there could be some room for the administration to highlight less inflation, so far, than economists predicted in response to his tariff policies, but not to claim no inflation.’  The article therefore concludes that Trump’s assertion of ‘no inflation’ is inaccurate by both the CPI and the Fed’s 2 % target, and that inflation has been climbing rather than easing for the last four months.

title: Trump Said He Would End Inflation on Day 1 of His Presidency  --  See Where We Stand Now
content: Donald Trump promised to 'end inflation on Day One' during an October rally in Saginaw, Michigan. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the annual CPI inflation rate averaged 2.65% from January to August 2025, above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. Inflation fell from 3.0% in January to 2.3% in April, but rebounded to 2.9% in August. A Goldman Sachs analysis shared with Bloomberg found that only 22% of the higher cost of imported goods was passed to consumers through June, with a projected rise to 67% if tariff policies continue. August CPI data showed grocery prices up 0.6% (largest in three years), apparel and audiovisual up 0.5%, car parts up 0.6%, and coffee 20% higher than a year ago; overall prices rose 0.4%, the largest monthly gain since December. Trump claimed on September 8 that 'We have no inflation. Prices are down on just about everything,' but the data suggests inflation is reaccelerating, possibly due to tariffs.

title: Americans Expect Inflation To Be Far Higher Than It Really Is, Polling Shows
content: American voters consistently rank inflation as the top issue, but since Donald Trump took office in January 2025, public expectations have diverged sharply from actual inflation. In December 2024, under President Biden, respondents predicted 2.8% inflation versus the actual 2.7%, a narrow gap. By May 2025, five months into Trump’s second term, the public estimated 6.6% inflation while the CPI showed 2.4%, a widening gap of 4.2 percentage points. The University of Michigan’s survey asked, 'By about what percent do you expect prices to go up/down on the average, during the next 12 months?' The chart shows the average response over four years, with the red line indicating the actual CPI rate. Food prices rose rapidly post‑pandemic and have remained high, while house prices have continued to climb, contributing to inflation expectations. Trump’s attempts to remove Fed Chair Lisa Cook, the introduction of high tariffs, the decline in the dollar’s value (from 98 euro cents in January to 85 in August, a fall of about 15%), and the $4.5 trillion tax‑cut bill have all added to uncertainty. The Yale University Budget Lab estimates the bill will add $3 trillion to debt 2025‑2034 and $12.1 trillion 2025‑2055, potentially prompting higher borrowing costs and inflation. The article cites Paul Whiteley, professor at the University of Essex, noting that inflation expectations influence Trump’s job approval, which tracks closely with his overall approval. The data suggest that if inflation expectations remain high, it could hurt Trump and the Republican Party in the 2026 mid‑terms.

title: Inflation derailed Biden. Is Trump next?
content: New polling shows that President Trump's approval rating among Republicans has slipped, and his policies on inflation are not sitting well with Americans. About half of Americans expect inflation to increase in the next six months, and rising prices are a continued source of stress for voters. Trump is now as unpopular on inflation as Biden was in 2022, and Republicans need to beware the return of inflation. Trump's campaign promises to bring down prices may finally be catching up to him, and a new report from Moody's Analytics predicts that his policies will slow U.S. growth and push up inflation, but stop short of an outright recession. 'It's not yet stagflation but it's edging that way,' said Moody's Justin Begley.

title: More Signs of Distress in Trump Economy as Inflation, Jobless Claims Rise | Common Dreams
content: The latest U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) data released on Thursday shows overall inflation at 2.9% year‑over‑year in August, with core inflation at 3.1%—the highest reading since January. Food prices rose 0.6% month‑over‑month and 2.7% year‑over‑year, a rebound after a period of easing. President Donald Trump said in a radio interview, 'We have no inflation. Prices are down on just about everything.' Economists noted the rebound in grocery prices, with Ben Casselman observing, 'Grocery prices are once again rising relatively rapidly.' Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, highlighted that coffee was 21% more expensive than a year ago, living‑room and dining‑room furniture rose 10% YoY, and toilet paper increased 5% YoY, adding, 'The middle‑class squeeze from tariffs is here.' Mike Konczal of the Economic Security Project said the data shows inflation is broadening, with nearly 60% of items experiencing at least a 3% annualized price increase over the last month—the highest percentage seen in years. The BLS also reported that jobless claims rose to 263,000 last week, above the 235,000 forecast and the highest total in nearly four years, prompting Long to warn that this is just the beginning of a downturn and that 'Cost cutting' is back among CEOs, signaling more layoffs. The article presents data and direct quotes without overt editorializing.
